At the end of a street that appeared on no map, there was a shop that sold beginnings.

Not grand beginnings, necessarily. Those were expensive and prone to disappointment. Most customers came for smaller things: the first sentence of an apology, the courage to open a long-delayed letter, the moment before a hand reaches for another hand.

The shopkeeper kept these in glass jars. They glowed faintly, especially on rainy days.

One evening, a woman came in and asked for a new life.

The shopkeeper considered her for a moment, then brought out a jar no larger than a thimble.

Inside was a single golden speck.

“That’s all?” she asked.

“It’s a Tuesday morning,” he said. “You wake up, make tea, and call your sister.”

The woman looked disappointed, but she bought it.

Years later, she returned with her sister. They argued cheerfully about the directions, then stood outside the shop window, trying to remember what had once been there.
